title: What should you ask first in an M&A case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in an M&A case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first why the client wants to buy, because the reason (growth, cost savings, new capabilities, blocking a rival) decides what the deal must deliver and what a fair price is. The trap is ignoring integration risk and forgetting that not buying, or buying something else, is always an option.
body:
The first question to ask

Why does the client want to buy this company?

A buyer chasing cost savings will judge the deal on overlapping costs it can remove. One buying a new product or capability will judge it on how fast it can sell that through its own customers. One worried about a competitor may accept a higher price to keep the target out of a rival's hands. The rationale tells you which numbers matter, so get it before you open any framework.

How to build your structure

  • The target on its own: its market, its performance against peers, its standalone value.
  • Synergies: revenue and cost, minus one-off integration costs.
  • Can we make it work? Funding, integration and culture, competition regulators.
  • Price: price against value to us; other targets; building or partnering instead.

The full tree is in the acquisition (M&A) framework.

Worked example: should we buy the competitor?

A client earning $5M a year of operating profit is considering a smaller competitor for $30M. The target earns $3M of operating profit. The client thinks it can save $1M a year by combining the two, but integration will cost $4M once.

1. The target on its own

$30M ÷ $3M is 10x operating profit. Is that $3M sustainable? Check its trend, its biggest customers and how much it needs to spend each year on equipment and stock. This is a quick screen, not a valuation.

2. Synergies

With $1M of savings the target is worth $4M a year to the client, so the price falls to 7.5x. Add the $4M integration bill and the client pays $34M for $4M a year: 8.5x. Test the $1M line by line. If it depends on closing two sites, can delivery times and service hold?

3. What is it worth to us?

Suppose, for illustration, that similar businesses sell for about 10x operating profit. Then the target is worth 10 × $4M − $4M = $36M to this client, $6M above the price. But if only half the savings arrive, value is 10 × $3.5M − $4M = $31M, and almost all of that headroom is gone. With no savings, it is $26M: the client would overpay by $4M.

So the answer is a walk-away price (around $31M to $36M depending on confidence in the savings) and a due diligence question: which of the savings can we prove before signing?

The trap most people fall into

Treating a profitable target as a good deal. Profit says nothing about whether the price is right, whether the savings will arrive, or whether staff and customers will stay through the integration. And many candidates never mention the do-nothing option.

Weak: "The target makes $3M a year and the market is growing, so it's a good acquisition."
Strong: "At $30M, the deal only pays if most of the $1M of savings arrive. I'd set a walk-away price of about $31M and make the site closures the first thing due diligence tests."

Two prompts to try

A sportswear brand wants to buy a fast-growing running-shoe start-up.

Show the answer
  • Rationale: entry to performance running; technology or brand it cannot build quickly.
  • Target: growth rate, margins, loyalty of its customers, founder dependence.
  • Synergies: selling through the buyer's stores and wholesale partners; cheaper sourcing and manufacturing.
  • Risks and price: losing the brand's appeal inside a big company; price against build or partner.

Where to start: revenue synergies. Most of the value depends on the buyer's distribution growing the brand.

The trap: assuming the start-up's growth continues unchanged after the founders leave.

A hospital group is considering buying a chain of physiotherapy clinics.

Show the answer
  • Rationale: keep patients after surgery; new revenue stream.
  • Target: clinic profits, utilisation of therapists, payer mix.
  • Synergies: referrals from the group's surgeons; shared booking and back office.
  • Feasibility: retaining therapists; regulatory or referral rules; integration of systems.

Where to start: referrals. How many of the group's patients need physio, and how many already go elsewhere?

The trap: counting referral revenue without checking whether therapists will stay.
